what_its_for: Obeticholic acid is used to treat a liver disease called Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC). PBC causes damage to the small bile ducts in your liver over time. This medicine helps protect your liver and slow down the disease, especially when used together with another medicine called ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), or alone if you cannot take UDCA.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with or without food. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablet. It is important to take this medicine exactly as your doctor tells you.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 5 mg once a day. After 3 months, your doctor may increase your dose to 10 mg once a day if your body is responding well and you are tolerating the medicine. If you have more advanced liver problems, your doctor may start you on a lower schedule such as 5 mg once a week and slowly increase it. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store obeticholic acid tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from moisture, heat, and light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking bile acid sequestrants (medicines like cholestyramine, colestipol, or colesevelam used to lower cholesterol) at the same time as obeticholic acid. If you take these medicines, take obeticholic acid at least 4 to 6 hours before or after them. Avoid drinking alcohol or taking other medicines that can harm your liver without talking to your doctor first. Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you notice: yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice), stomach pain especially in the upper right area, dark urine, light-colored stools, unusual tiredness or weakness, nausea or vomiting that does not go away, confusion or difficulty thinking clearly, severe itching that is getting worse, swelling in your legs or belly, or any signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face or throat. These may be signs that your liver disease is getting worse.
when_it_works: You may not feel any different while taking obeticholic acid because liver disease often does not cause obvious symptoms early on. Your doctor will check your blood tests (especially a liver enzyme called ALP and bilirubin) every few months to see if the medicine is working. Improvements in blood tests are usually seen within the first 3 to 6 months. It is important to keep taking this medicine even if you feel well, because it is working to protect your liver over the long term.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as its safety in these situations is not fully known. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is usually needed for older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children. Liver problems: If you have moderate to severe liver disease (also called decompensated cirrhosis), your doctor will prescribe a much lower and more cautious dosing schedule and will watch you very carefully, as this medicine can cause serious liver harm in people with advanced liver disease.
